https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/betacord.2eb960d3bedfa00ab18da90456d2c4038768a0aa9ba7f4a101e49174a877eb8f_hu_df817b6e0638f0e6.webp 950w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="950" height="587" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/betacord.2eb960d3bedfa00ab18da90456d2c4038768a0aa9ba7f4a101e49174a877eb8f_hu_d942e4d9c2c72a90.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">A typical Betamax recorder. This and similar appliances influenced the international design of the NES. I spotted this particular one at The Centre for Computing History (Cambridge, UK) when I visited in August 2024.</figcaption></figure><p>Nintendo ended up shipping lots of different variants of the same console across the world <sup id="bibref:1"><a href="#bib:general-variants" role="doc-biblioref">[1]</a></sup> and even though they all share the same architecture, many look dramatically different and some may include built-in accessories. So, to keep it simple for this article, I’ll focus on the two most popular revisions:</p><ul><li>The <strong>Family Computer</strong> (known as <em>Famicom</em>) was the first incarnation, but was only released in Japan. This toy-looking design features two non-removable controllers (from which the second controller bundles an internal microphone), a front socket for the light gun (called <em>Zapper</em>), RF video out (using NTSC-J signal) and extra pins in the cartridge slot to expand the audio capabilities.</li><li>The <strong>Nintendo Entertainment System</strong> (known as <em>NES</em>) was the redesigned edition for western audiences living in North America, Europe and Oceania; with a look and mechanism that matches the common VHS/Betamax player. On the technical side, the controllers are now detachable (and microphone-lacking) and the video out has been improved with extra NTSC/PAL composite RCA connectors, although the audio expansion has been replaced with an anti-piracy subsystem. To top it off, the bottom of the case seals an ‘expansion port’ that was left unused, along with extra cartridge pins that communicate to that port <sup id="bibref:2"><a href="#bib:general-cartridge" role="doc-biblioref">[2]</a></sup>.</li></ul><p>Because the author grew up with the ‘NES’ name, I will default to using that term to refer to the console in general, but I will switch to ‘Famicom’ when referring to unique capabilities only found in the Japanese variant.</p><hr><h2 id="cpu">CPU</h2><p>The NES’s CPU is a <strong>Ricoh 2A03</strong> <sup id="bibref:3"><a href="#bib:cpu-cpu" role="doc-biblioref">[3]</a></sup>, which is based on the popular 8-bit <strong>MOS Technology 6502</strong> and runs at <strong>1.79 MHz</strong> (or 1.66 MHz in PAL systems). This is the central component that executes the code inside the game cartridge.</p><h3 id="a-bit-of-context">A bit of context</h3><p>To understand the circuitry residing inside the NES’ motherboard, we must first take a look at the state of the industry at the time. Interestingly, the CPU market in the late 70s and early 80s was quite diverse.</p><figure class="side-by-side"><figure class="toleft"><a class="toleft" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/pet.fb214c0d0cdb25a7353240a06f6f6534614d945e1886b4b7002f036e193f3c47.webp"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/pet.fb214c0d0cdb25a7353240a06f6f6534614d945e1886b4b7002f036e193f3c47.webp"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="900" height="634" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/pet.fb214c0d0cdb25a7353240a06f6f6534614d945e1886b4b7002f036e193f3c47_hu_91e54ab5b39b73dc.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">A Commodore PET, carrying a 6502 CPU.</figcaption></figure><figure class="toright"><a class="toright" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/tandy.92e1450204bbb984bd7e04d23c9242c5c47f735e8519123a4013fbff1615a7f8.webp"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/tandy.92e1450204bbb984bd7e04d23c9242c5c47f735e8519123a4013fbff1615a7f8.webp"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="900" height="634" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/tandy.92e1450204bbb984bd7e04d23c9242c5c47f735e8519123a4013fbff1615a7f8_hu_45003284d1be99db.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">A Tandy TRS-80, carrying a Z80 CPU.</figcaption></figure><figcaption class="caption">The panorama of late-70s computers, also provided by The Centre for Computing History (Cambridge, UK).</figcaption></figure><p>If you were a startup aiming to build an affordable microcomputer for the western world, you had plenty of options available:</p><ul><li>The <strong>Intel 8080</strong> (1974): A popular CPU featured in the MITS Altair 8800, the first ‘personal’ computer. It comes with a modest 8-bit data bus, a 16-bit address bus (enough to handle the necessary memory), and seven 8-bit registers. With capabilities like this, a line was drawn between the simple calculator and an actual computer.</li><li>The <strong>Zilog Z80</strong> (1976): Displeased with Intel’s direction and lack of investment in their CPU division, former engineers of the 8080 started their own company to produce an ‘unofficial’ successor, enhanced with more instructions, registers, and internal components. To top it off, it was sold at a lower price and could still execute 8080 programs <sup id="bibref:4"><a href="#bib:cpu-re_1977" role="doc-biblioref">[4]</a></sup>. The new CPU was well received by British firms Amstrad and Sinclair, as well as the Japanese <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/master-system/">Sega</a>, among others.</li><li>The <strong>Motorola 6800</strong> (1974): Another 8-bit CPU designed around the same time. While a direct competitor of the 8080, the 6800 was programmed using a more sophisticated instruction set, albeit running at a slower clock speed <sup id="bibref:5"><a href="#bib:cpu-arizona" role="doc-biblioref">[5]</a></sup>. Nevertheless, many do-it-yourself computer kits, synthesisers, and all-in-one computers included the 6800.</li></ul><p>Faced with similar setbacks that Intel’s employees went through, engineers at Motorola grew frustrated with the company’s lack of interest in capitalising on the potential of the 6800 <sup id="bibref:6"><a href="#bib:cpu-austin" role="doc-biblioref">[6]</a></sup>. So, they joined a small but ambitious silicon firm, <strong>MOS</strong>, where they worked on a redesigned version of the 6800 - the <strong>MOS 6502</strong>. While incompatible with the rest, the new chip was much, <em>much</em> cheaper to produce <sup id="bibref:7"><a href="#bib:cpu-summary_costs" role="doc-biblioref">[7]</a></sup> <sup id="bibref:8"><a href="#bib:cpu-re_1981" role="doc-biblioref">[8]</a></sup>, and it was only a matter of time before iconic computer makers (Commodore, Tandy, Apple, Atari, Acorn, and so forth) chose the 6502 to power their machines.</p><p>Back in Japan, Nintendo needed something inexpensive yet familiar to develop for, so they selected the 6502. <strong>Ricoh</strong>, their CPU supplier, successfully produced a 6502-compatible clone.</p><h3 id="core-functionality">Core functionality</h3><p>To understand how capable this console is, let’s first check what the original MOS 6502 offers:</p><ul><li>The <strong>6502 ISA</strong>: MOS wanted to offer drastic improvements at the cost of compatibility with third-parties (especially Motorola) <sup id="bibref:9"><a href="#bib:cpu-arizona" role="doc-biblioref">[9]</a></sup>. Thus, the 6502 instruction set still handles <strong>8-bit</strong> words like the 6800 and others, but its programming is not cross-compatible.</li><li>An <strong>8-bit data bus</strong> and a <strong>16-bit address bus</strong>. This was the typical combination for microprocessors of that era. Basically, it allows to operate data in chunks of eight bits without running out of memory locations (at least, too quickly).<ul><li>On paper, 16-bit addresses means the 8-bit CPU will need extra cycles to process the extra size. However, thanks to MOS’s new addressing modes (explained further down), these penalties were alleviated without requiring too much circuitry.</li></ul></li><li><strong>Three general-purpose registers</strong> (<code>X</code>, <code>Y</code> and <code>A</code>), which may look constrained when compared to <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/master-system/#cpu">larger register files</a>. This decision reduces costs but also means the CPU would need to move memory around more frequently. With the 6502, <code>X</code> and <code>Y</code> are called ‘index registers’ and are used to address memory, while <code>A</code> is directly connected to the ALU and dedicated to arithmetic operations.<ul><li>By comparison, the Motorola 6800 has two accumulator registers and only one index register, which allows for a simpler instruction set.</li></ul></li><li>An <strong>8-bit Arithmetic Logic Unit</strong> (ALU), which comes as no surprise for an 8-bit CPU, but it’s worth pointing out that others like the Zilog Z80 came with an <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/master-system/#cpu">4-bit ALU instead</a>.</li><li>An <strong>8-bit stack pointer</strong>: This is usually beyond the scope of this analysis, but I wanted to highlight it due to its significant deviation from Motorola’s design. As mentioned before, the address bus is 16-bit, so a memory-dependent component like the stack pointer should ideally match that size. However, MOS opted to halve the requirement and store the stack within a fixed memory range. Nevertheless, it was a clever cost-saving measure, as it encouraged developers to adopt efficient programming techniques to maximise the stack space.</li><li><strong>13 addressing modes</strong>. Thanks to the inclusion of two index registers, programs can choose between many formats for accessing memory. Some are optimised for zero-page addressing (the first 256 bytes of memory), while others encode a lookup address to retrieve the actual address dynamically. In the end, this helped save as many memory cycles as possible, at the cost of complexity.<ul><li>By comparison, the 6800 and its single index register only offer seven addressing modes, with no equivalent for the flexible types.</li></ul></li></ul><p>As you can see, the remarkable engineering behind the 6502 allowed MOS to sell a compelling product at an extremely affordable price.</p><h4 id="ricohs-licensing-enigma">Ricoh’s licensing enigma</h4><p><em>How</em> Ricoh managed to clone the 6502 isn’t clear to this day. One would expect MOS to have licensed the chip design to Ricoh, but there are many contradictions to this:</p><ul><li>Both Ricoh’s and MOS’s variants feature the same layout, but Ricoh’s contains severed buses (disabling certain functions) <sup id="bibref:10"><a href="#bib:cpu-differences" role="doc-biblioref">[10]</a></sup>. I go into more detail later.</li><li>A document explicitly stating that MOS licensed the 6502 to Ricoh is yet to be found.</li><li>An article published in 2008 by Nikkei Trendy states that Ricoh licensed from Rockwell, an authorised chip manufacturer <sup id="bibref:11"><a href="#bib:cpu-trendi" role="doc-biblioref">[11]</a></sup>. However, it’s debatable whether a second source was able to provide IP to a third party, much less with MOS’s approval.</li><li>It wouldn’t be the first time Nintendo got away with circumventing IP rights, as <em>Ikegami Tsushinki v. Nintendo</em> ruled in Japan that Nintendo didn’t own the code of the original Donkey Kong <sup id="bibref:12"><a href="#bib:cpu-dk" role="doc-biblioref">[12]</a></sup>.</li></ul><h4 id="scrapped-functions">Scrapped functions</h4><p>The Ricoh 2A03 omits the <strong>Binary-Coded Decimal</strong> (BCD) mode originally included in the 6502 <sup id="bibref:13"><a href="#bib:cpu-visualbcd" role="doc-biblioref">[13]</a></sup>. BCD encodes each decimal digit of a number as a separate 4-bit binary. The 6502 uses 8-bit ‘words’ - meaning that each word stores two decimal digits.</p><p>As an example for the curious, the decimal number <code>42</code> is represented as:</p><ul><li><code>0010 1010</code> in binary.</li><li><code>0100 0010</code> in BCD.</li></ul><p>We could go on and on talking about it, but to give an outline: BCD is useful for applications that require treating each decimal place separately (for instance, a digital clock). However, it requires more storage since each 8-bit word can only encode up to the decimal number <code>99</code> - whereas traditional binary can encode up to <code>255</code>.</p><p>In any case, Ricoh deliberately broke BCD mode in its chip by severing the control lines that activate it. This was presumably done to avoid paying royalties to MOS, since BCD was patented by them (and the legislation that enabled copyrighting integrated circuit layouts in the United States wasn’t enacted until 1984 <sup id="bibref:14"><a href="#bib:cpu-protection_act" role="doc-biblioref">[14]</a></sup>).</p><h3 id="memory">Memory</h3><p>Both Ricoh 2A03 and MOS 6502 feature an <strong>8-bit data bus</strong> and a <strong>16-bit address bus</strong>, which allow them to access up to <strong>64 KB of memory</strong>. So, how did Nintendo fill that memory space?</p><p>On one side, the motherboard contains a chip providing <strong>2 KB of Static RAM</strong> (SRAM) <sup id="bibref:15"><a href="#bib:cpu-sample_ram" role="doc-biblioref">[15]</a></sup>. Nintendo calls this area ‘Work RAM’ (WRAM) and can be used to store:</p><ul><li>Variables for handling the game state and/or to look up information.</li><li>The ‘stack’, which temporarily saves register values while the CPU is executing subroutines.</li><li>A ‘buffer area’ so the CPU can copy large data between two locations.</li></ul><p>On the other side, the components of the system are <strong>memory-mapped</strong> <sup id="bibref:16"><a href="#bib:cpu-cpu_map" role="doc-biblioref">[16]</a></sup>, meaning that they are accessed using memory addresses and therefore occupy part of the CPU’s address space. Consequently, the Ricoh 2A03’s memory space is filled with addresses pointing to the game cartridge, WRAM, the PPU, the APU and two controllers (don’t worry about each component, as they are explained throughout this article).</p><h4 id="segmentation-fault">Segmentation Fault</h4><p>Inherited from MOS’ design, this console also features a special ‘anomaly’ called <strong>Open Bus</strong>: If an instruction tries to read from an unmapped or invalid address, the last value read is supplied instead <sup id="bibref:17"><a href="#bib:nes-open_bus" role="doc-biblioref">[17]</a></sup>. If this goes unhandled by the program, execution may continue in an unpredictable state.</p><h4 id="cartridgegame-data">Cartridge/game data</h4><p>Just in case you don’t know, NES games are distributed in the form of <strong>cartridges</strong>, and the cartridge’s buses connect directly to the CPU.</p><p>Nintendo wired up the cartridge lines in a way that only 49120 Bytes (~ 49.97 KB) of cartridge data can be accessed <sup id="bibref:18"><a href="#bib:cpu-cpu_map" role="doc-biblioref">[18]</a></sup>. Now, what do I mean by ‘cartridge data’? Well, any chip connected to those buses, for instance:</p><ul><li>A <strong>Program ROM</strong> where the game’s program resides. This excludes the graphics data, as you’ll later see in the ‘Graphics’ section. Naturally and unlike the other chips, this one is mandatory.</li><li><strong>RAM chips</strong> to extend WRAM.</li><li>A <strong>battery-packed RAM chip</strong> to store saves.</li></ul><p>The existence of different combinations stems from the fact that the CPU doesn’t care about what kind of component it is reading from; it only sees memory locations. So, it is up to game studios to choose (or devise) a feasible layout to fit in their game.</p><div class="tabs nested centered-container"><ul class="tab-links nested"><li id="nestedtab-1-1-original-link" class="active"><a href="#nestedtab-1-1-original">Original</a></li><li id="nestedtab-1-2-marked-link"><a href="#nestedtab-1-2-marked">Marked</a></li></ul><figure class="tab active nested" id="nestedtab-1-1-original"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/nrom.b4be7609d15f9dfee3498325efbfacc75efc9629ea841c18d6288902eede7a71.png"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/nrom.b4be7609d15f9dfee3498325efbfacc75efc9629ea841c18d6288902eede7a71_hu_51c059125d990a9c.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/nrom.b4be7609d15f9dfee3498325efbfacc75efc9629ea841c18d6288902eede7a71_hu_d62499662ebc0901.webp 699w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="699" height="288" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/nrom.b4be7609d15f9dfee3498325efbfacc75efc9629ea841c18d6288902eede7a71.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">PCB of Super Mario Bros <sup id="bibref:19"><a href="#bib:photography-nrom" role="doc-biblioref">[19]</a></sup>.</figcaption></figure><figure class="tab nested" id="nestedtab-1-2-marked"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/nrom_marked.272d917f53f92b089c20b0a104fb8c2f73cfd0b5516b5d0b1fe88fca9ef24fd1.png"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/nrom_marked.272d917f53f92b089c20b0a104fb8c2f73cfd0b5516b5d0b1fe88fca9ef24fd1_hu_34fbd30507972d1e.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/nrom_marked.272d917f53f92b089c20b0a104fb8c2f73cfd0b5516b5d0b1fe88fca9ef24fd1_hu_c5d735466efaa222.webp 699w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="699" height="288" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/nrom_marked.272d917f53f92b089c20b0a104fb8c2f73cfd0b5516b5d0b1fe88fca9ef24fd1.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">The same PCB with important parts labelled. The meaning of the ‘Lockout’ chip is explained in the ‘Anti-piracy’ section.</figcaption></figure></div><p>For example, Nintendo’s ‘Super Mario Bros’ used a layout they call <em>NES-NROM-256</em> and consists of 32 KB of program ROM and 8 KB of ‘Character ROM’ for graphics (we’ll see more about it in the ‘Graphics’ section) <sup id="bibref:20"><a href="#bib:cpu-nrom" role="doc-biblioref">[20]</a></sup>. <em>NES-NROM-256</em> was also prepared to house up to 3 KB of extra WRAM, though the game doesn’t make use of it.</p><h4 id="going-beyond-existing-capabilities">Going beyond existing capabilities</h4><p>One of the major limitations of 16-bit address buses (affecting 3rd and 4th-generation consoles) is their compact address space. Nowadays, 32-bit computers can address up to 4 GB of memory (and 64-bit machines lavishly enjoy up to 16 exabytes), so this is no longer a concern, but back then, the NES only had a 64 KB address space, and a significant portion was consumed by the memory-mapped hardware (something <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/master-system/#accessing-the-rest-of-the-components">competitors avoided</a>).</p><p>So, did this mean that game studios could only develop games that stayed within the 49.97 KB limit? Absolutely not! If history has taught us anything, it is that there’s always a clever solution to a challenging problem, and this issue was tackled with a <strong>Mapper</strong>.</p><div class="tabs nested centered-container"><ul class="tab-links nested"><li id="nestedtab-2-1-with-mapper-link" class="active"><a href="#nestedtab-2-1-with-mapper">With mapper</a></li><li id="nestedtab-2-2-without-mapper-link"><a href="#nestedtab-2-2-without-mapper">Without mapper</a></li></ul><figure class="tab active nested" id="nestedtab-2-1-with-mapper"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/_diagrams/mapper/mapper.ce712cf90024e048a2a2566df581e02584e11d7684f986fa508ce746a3e09cbc.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="738" height="338" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/_diagrams/mapper/mapper.ce712cf90024e048a2a2566df581e02584e11d7684f986fa508ce746a3e09cbc.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Simplified representation of how a mapper extends the addressing capabilities of the CPU. With the inclusion of a mapper, the CPU can access extra banks (groups of addresses) of a large Program ROM. Although the game/program has the new task of manually switching between banks whenever needed.</figcaption></figure><figure class="tab nested" id="nestedtab-2-2-without-mapper"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/_diagrams/mapper/no_mapper.912a9dbb44efa4b4e599f53960b045930d7dfb6ddf071b4f3a94d02067f5c153.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="481" height="242" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/_diagrams/mapper/no_mapper.912a9dbb44efa4b4e599f53960b045930d7dfb6ddf071b4f3a94d02067f5c153.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">The same setup but without a mapper installed. While simpler and inexpensive, the CPU can only access a finite number of banks.</figcaption></figure></div><p>A mapper is an extra chip included in the cartridge that sits between the memory chips and the console’s address lines. Its primary job is to extend the address space, allowing developers to fit more chips. This is achieved through <strong>bank switching</strong>: memory addresses are grouped into banks, and the mapper provides switches (controlled via memory addresses) to alternate between them. Now, the CPU still perceives the same amount of memory, so it is the game (programmed with a mapper present) in charge of operating it. Due to their cost-effectiveness, mappers were the order of the day in 80s-to-early-90s technology.</p><div class="tabs nested centered-container"><ul class="tab-links nested"><li id="nestedtab-3-1-original-link" class="active"><a href="#nestedtab-3-1-original">Original</a></li><li id="nestedtab-3-2-marked-link"><a href="#nestedtab-3-2-marked">Marked</a></li></ul><figure class="tab active nested" id="nestedtab-3-1-original"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/tsrom.b8bbb5d13834500682896fda3682e41a70aca6a00bde14c9e0e7df04e9537e55.png"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/tsrom.b8bbb5d13834500682896fda3682e41a70aca6a00bde14c9e0e7df04e9537e55_hu_e82c98a5a12edd65.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/tsrom.b8bbb5d13834500682896fda3682e41a70aca6a00bde14c9e0e7df04e9537e55_hu_2ce02a296eea5581.webp 692w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="692" height="409" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/tsrom.b8bbb5d13834500682896fda3682e41a70aca6a00bde14c9e0e7df04e9537e55.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">PCB of Super Mario Bros 2 <sup id="bibref:21"><a href="#bib:photography-tsrom" role="doc-biblioref">[21]</a></sup>. Super Mario Bros 3 also uses this layout but bundles a 256 KB Program ROM instead.</figcaption></figure><figure class="tab nested" id="nestedtab-3-2-marked"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/tsrom_marked.d7d3bae32bf8ea63384aef5eb331a91956fbba1cd1f303f6b11aab74b0a7a957.png"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/tsrom_marked.d7d3bae32bf8ea63384aef5eb331a91956fbba1cd1f303f6b11aab74b0a7a957_hu_752008f5fe8f8276.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/tsrom_marked.d7d3bae32bf8ea63384aef5eb331a91956fbba1cd1f303f6b11aab74b0a7a957_hu_a698ccc7d9dac114.webp 692w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="692" height="409" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/tsrom_marked.d7d3bae32bf8ea63384aef5eb331a91956fbba1cd1f303f6b11aab74b0a7a957.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">The same picture with important parts labelled. At first, I thought the extra WRAM was for storing saves, but then I realised there are no saves in this game (and there isn’t a battery either). In reality, that RAM chip is used to store a decompressed level.</figcaption></figure></div><p>Back to the NES, games like ‘Super Mario Bros 2’ and ‘Super Mario Bros 3’ shipped with the ‘MMC3’ mapper (made by Nintendo) in their cartridges. For comparison, MMC3 provided up to 512 KB of space for the Program ROM, up to 256 KB for Character memory and up to 8 KB for extra WRAM <sup id="bibref:22"><a href="#bib:cpu-mmc3" role="doc-biblioref">[22]</a></sup>. You can now see why ‘Super Mario Bros 3’ differs significantly in quality compared to the first instalment.</p><p>All in all, while this console may appear limited while examining its internal features, Nintendo made sure it could adapt as technology evolves. On the other side, while this technique helped to keep the costs down of the console, it shifted part of the burden to the game cartridge. So, game quality and cartridge costs were two concerns game studios had to balance.</p><hr><h2 id="graphics">Graphics</h2><p>Graphics are generated by a proprietary chip called the <strong>Picture Processing Unit</strong> (PPU). This is one of the chips that gives the NES an <em>identity</em>. To put it another way, since anyone could pick up a 6502 at a hardware store, why is the NES any different from, say, an Apple II or a Commodore 64? Well, what distinguishes the NES from other machines are the chips that surround the CPU: the PPU and the APU. These make up the NES’ unique graphics and audio capabilities, respectively.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/ppu_chip.8fcd47f5d796ddef2bb4d8baa534306df6d7b81668b4af6b90157f0d32194da6.webp"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/ppu_chip.8fcd47f5d796ddef2bb4d8baa534306df6d7b81668b4af6b90157f0d32194da6.webp"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="800" height="302" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/ppu_chip.8fcd47f5d796ddef2bb4d8baa534306df6d7b81668b4af6b90157f0d32194da6_hu_6e8e279b6737c82.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">The European PPU chip on my NES’ motherboard.</figcaption></figure><p>That being said, the PPU renders 2D graphics called <strong>sprites</strong> and <strong>backgrounds</strong>, outputting the result to the video signal.</p><h3 id="organising-the-content">Organising the content</h3><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/_diagrams/ppu.8ca545d7ec1fbf59e628d4b670b565f94757f79b656f35f1140261794b4014f4.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="1039" height="536" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/_diagrams/ppu.8ca545d7ec1fbf59e628d4b670b565f94757f79b656f35f1140261794b4014f4.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Memory architecture of the PPU.</figcaption></figure><p>To render something on the screen, the PPU must know <em>which</em> graphics to draw, <em>where</em> on the screen to place them, and <em>how</em> to draw them (i.e., which palette to use).</p><p>To answer these questions, the PPU came pre-programmed with a different memory layout that looks for specific types of data:</p><ul><li>Graphics data is pulled from the game cartridge, which contains a dedicated chip called <strong>Character memory</strong> that stores the 2D drawings (called <strong>tiles</strong>) organised into a data structure named <strong>Pattern table</strong>. Character memory materialises in the form of ‘Read-Only Memory’ (ROM) or ‘Random-Access Memory’ (RAM), depending on whether the game ships with an immutable set of graphics or the CPU must intervene, respectively.<ul><li>The PPU addresses <strong>up to 8 KB</strong> of Character memory organised into two groups of 4 KB each.</li></ul></li><li>Meta-data telling the PPU ‘where’ and ‘how’ to draw graphics is found in other areas:<ul><li>The motherboard houses <strong>2 KB of SRAM</strong> specifically for graphics-related data. Nintendo calls this space <strong>Video RAM</strong> (VRAM), and it stores two data structures called <strong>Nametables</strong>.</li><li>The PPU embeds <strong>256 bytes</strong> of DRAM to store the <strong>Object Attribute Memory</strong> (OAM).</li><li>Lastly, the PPU also bundles <strong>4 bytes</strong> of memory to define colour palettes.</li></ul></li></ul><p>Don’t worry about the new terminology; the meanings of these data structures are discussed step by step in the following paragraphs.</p><h3 id="constructing-the-frame">Constructing the frame</h3><p>As with its contemporaries, this chip is designed for the behaviour of a CRT display. There is no frame buffer as such: <strong>the PPU will render in step with the CRT’s beam</strong>, building the image on the fly.</p><p>The PPU draws frames with a fixed dimension of <strong>256x240 pixels</strong> <sup id="bibref:23"><a href="#bib:graphics-overscan" role="doc-biblioref">[23]</a></sup>. Alas, due to the discrepancies in analogue video standards across the world, the image will differ in appearance depending on the region of the appliance (NTSC or PAL) from which it is displayed. In a nutshell, NTSC televisions will crop the top and bottom edges to accommodate overscan (only ~224 scan-lines are visible), so these edges are considered ‘danger zones’ by developers when deciding where to place elements in the game. On the other hand, PAL tellies won’t crop the edges but will show extra black bars to fill the taller signal (PAL uses 288 scan-lines).</p><p>Behind the scenes, the frame output by the PPU is composed of two different layers. For demonstration purposes, let’s use <em>Super Mario Bros.</em> to show how this works:</p><div class="tabs"><ul class="tab-links"><li id="tab-1-1-tiles-link" class="active"><a href="#tab-1-1-tiles">Tiles</a></li><li id="tab-1-2-background-layer-link"><a href="#tab-1-2-background-layer">Background Layer</a></li><li id="tab-1-3-sprite-layer-link"><a href="#tab-1-3-sprite-layer">Sprite Layer</a></li><li id="tab-1-4-background-split-link"><a href="#tab-1-4-background-split">Background Split</a></li><li id="tab-1-5-result-link"><a href="#tab-1-5-result">Result</a></li></ul><div class="tab-content"><div class="tab active body-side" id="tab-1-1-tiles"><h4 id="tab-1-1-tiles" class="tab-title">Tiles</h4><figure class="tabs nested float-side pixel desktop-margined"><ul class="tab-links nested"><li id="nestedtab-4-1-all-link" class="active"><a href="#nestedtab-4-1-all">All</a></li><li id="nestedtab-4-2-single-link"><a href="#nestedtab-4-2-single">Single</a></li></ul><figure class="tab active nested" id="nestedtab-4-1-all"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/ppu_mario/chr_map.85c856cefd8daa4752b44b0fc04c9bc3e60ece2851f932bf64431dee293f54d2.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="128" height="256" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/ppu_mario/chr_map.85c856cefd8daa4752b44b0fc04c9bc3e60ece2851f932bf64431dee293f54d2.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Two pattern tables with multiple tiles squashed together.</figcaption></figure><figure class="tab nested" id="nestedtab-4-2-single"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="8" height="8" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/ppu_mario/single.cd333403bda182a98bc72773125dadee3055e8dbce200823039e09b7e12996f7.png" loading="eager"></picture><figcaption class="caption">A single tile.</figcaption></figure><figcaption class="caption group">Tiles Found in Character ROM (for demonstration purposes a default palette is being used).</figcaption></figure><p>To begin with, the PPU uses <strong>tiles</strong> as a basic ingredient for producing sprites and backgrounds.</p><p>The NES defines tiles as basic <strong>8x8 pixel maps</strong>, these are stored in <strong>Character memory</strong> (residing in the game cartridge) and organised into a big data structure called <strong>Pattern Table</strong> <sup id="bibref:24"><a href="#bib:graphics-rust" role="doc-biblioref">[24]</a></sup>. Each tile occupies 16 bytes, and a Pattern table houses 256 tiles <sup id="bibref:25"><a href="#bib:graphics-pattern" role="doc-biblioref">[25]</a></sup>. Since the PPU addresses up to 8 KB of Character memory, it can access up to two Pattern tables.</p><p>Inside a tile, each of its pixels is encoded using a 2-bit value, which references one of four colours from a palette. Programmers can define up to eight palettes (four for the background and four for sprites). The colours referenced on each palette point to a ‘master palette’ consisting of 64 colours <sup id="bibref:26"><a href="#bib:graphics-palettes" role="doc-biblioref">[26]</a></sup>, representing all the colours that this console can produce. Each palette is made of four colours, with one reserved for <code>transparent</code>.</p><p>To start drawing something on the screen, games populate a set of tables with references to tiles stored in Character memory. Each table is responsible for one layer (sprite or background) of the frame. Then, the PPU reads from those tables and composes the scan-lines that will be beamed by the CRT gun.</p><p>I will now explain how each layer/table works and how they differ in terms of functionality.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev pre">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-1-2-background-layer">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-1-2-background-layer"><h4 id="tab-1-2-background-layer" class="tab-title">Background Layer</h4><figure class="tabs nested float-side pixel"><ul class="tab-links nested"><li id="nestedtab-5-1-overall-link" class="active"><a href="#nestedtab-5-1-overall">Overall</a></li><li id="nestedtab-5-2-selected-link"><a href="#nestedtab-5-2-selected">Selected</a></li></ul><figure class="tab active nested" id="nestedtab-5-1-overall"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/ppu_mario/nametable.e0055ad58816fb592360356ed85e039010bf2d25f382922da0ec3c65f29c7153.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="512" height="480" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/ppu_mario/nametable.e0055ad58816fb592360356ed85e039010bf2d25f382922da0ec3c65f29c7153.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Visualised background map.</figcaption></figure><figure class="tab nested" id="nestedtab-5-2-selected"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/ppu_mario/nametable_marked.e0e520cc7636d1539f9798032e9c14882a79b49cadba9faf25bfece7ae19cbe3.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="512" height="480" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/ppu_mario/nametable_marked.e0e520cc7636d1539f9798032e9c14882a79b49cadba9faf25bfece7ae19cbe3.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Visualised background with selected area marked.</figcaption></figure><figcaption class="caption group">This background map is set up with vertical mirroring, which enables smooth horizontal scrolling. However, only the top half can be used.</figcaption></figure><p>The background layer is a 512x480 pixel map containing static tiles <sup id="bibref:27"><a href="#bib:graphics-nametables" role="doc-biblioref">[27]</a></sup>. You may recall that the viewable frame is much smaller, so the game decides which part of the layer is selected for display. Games can also shift the viewable area during gameplay; that’s how the <strong>scrolling effect</strong> is accomplished.</p><p>To save memory, groups of four tiles are combined into 16x16-pixel maps called <strong>blocks</strong>, in which all tiles share a colour palette.</p><p><strong>Nametables</strong> (stored in VRAM) specify which tiles to display in the background layer. The PPU looks for four 1024-byte Nametables, each one corresponding to a quadrant of the layer. However, only 2 KB of VRAM is available! Meaning that only two Nametables can be stored without additional hardware provided by the cartridge. Yet, the remaining two still have to be addressed somewhere: most games simply point the remaining two where the first two are (this is called <strong>mirroring</strong>).</p><p>Although this architecture may seem flawed at first, it was designed to minimise costs while ensuring simple <strong>expandability</strong>: if the game requires a wider background, just fit extra VRAM in the cartridge.</p><p>Moving on, the last bytes of each Nametable store a 64-byte <strong>Attribute table</strong> that specifies which colour palette is assigned to each block <sup id="bibref:28"><a href="#bib:graphics-attribute_table" role="doc-biblioref">[28]</a></sup>.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-1-1-tiles">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-1-3-sprite-layer">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-1-3-sprite-layer"><h4 id="tab-1-3-sprite-layer" class="tab-title">Sprite Layer</h4><figure class="float-side pixel"><a class="pixel" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/ppu_mario/sprite_layer.5be82835c348c3dff9873a74ab923877ff4b7bed75c333dbc4b38e190f3c7379.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="256" height="240" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/ppu_mario/sprite_layer.5be82835c348c3dff9873a74ab923877ff4b7bed75c333dbc4b38e190f3c7379.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Rendered sprite layer.</figcaption></figure><p>Sprites are tiles that can move around the screen. They can also overlap one another, or appear behind the background. The viewable graphic is determined by its priority value (similar to the concept of ‘layers’ in traditional graphic design software).</p><p>The <strong>Object Attribute Memory</strong> (OAM) table specifies which tiles will be used as sprites <sup id="bibref:29"><a href="#bib:graphics-oam" role="doc-biblioref">[29]</a></sup>. In addition to the tile index, each entry includes an (x,y) position and several attributes (colour palette, priority and flip flags). This table resides in a 256-byte DRAM located within the PPU chip.</p><p>The CPU can populate the OAM table, but this process can be slow in practice and risks corrupting the frame if not timed correctly. As a result, the PPU contains a small component called <strong>Direct Memory Access</strong> or ‘DMA’ which can be programmed (by altering the PPU’s registers) to fetch the table from WRAM. With DMA, the table is guaranteed to be uploaded when the next frame is drawn; however, the CPU will be halted during the transfer!</p><p>The PPU is limited to <strong>eight sprites per scan-line</strong> and up to <strong>64 sprites per frame</strong>. Luckily, the scan-line limit can be partially circumvented thanks to a technique called ‘OAM order rotation’, in which the game manually alters the order of entries in OAM. This makes the PPU render a different sprite set at each frame, and the speed of the CRT beam will trick the user into seeing more sprites than allowed. However, they will also appear to flicker on-screen.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-1-2-background-layer">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-1-4-background-split">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-1-4-background-split"><h4 id="tab-1-4-background-split" class="tab-title">Background Split</h4><figure class="float-side pixel"><a class="pixel" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/ppu_mario/split.7d72639126de3ef8b96b676e2322591454aa1e938420a85e261f295ae007ab92.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="256" height="240" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/ppu_mario/split.7d72639126de3ef8b96b676e2322591454aa1e938420a85e261f295ae007ab92.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Rendered background layer highlighting the two portions with different scrolling values defined. Only the second portion scrolls as Mario moves.</figcaption></figure><p>Before we move on, there’s an additional detail worth mentioning. If you play Super Mario Bros, you’ll notice that when Mario moves, the scene scrolls without a hitch. However, you’ll also observe that the top area (where the stats are) remains static <strong>even though both portions belong to the same background layer!</strong> So, what is happening here? Well, the game is altering the scrolling values mid-frame to show the overworld and the stats (residing in a fixed portion of the background) at the same time. The NES doesn’t provide this feature natively, but the game deduces the timings by observing the state of the PPU (manifested through its status register <sup id="bibref:30"><a href="#bib:graphics-ppustatus" role="doc-biblioref">[30]</a></sup>).</p><p>To accomplish this, games use a technique called <strong>Sprite 0 Hit</strong>. Super Mario Bros instructs the PPU to render a dummy sprite behind the coin, this happens to be the first sprite drawn within the frame. After the PPU beams it, it updates its status register with a flag to indicate that the first sprite (a.k.a ‘sprite 0’) has been drawn. Meanwhile, the game continuously checks mid-frame whether the sprite 0 status has been flagged (a.k.a ‘hit’). When this occurs, the game updates the scrolling value of the background table to align it with Mario’s position.</p><p>Overall, ‘Sprite 0 Hit’ is a very delicate procedure, as it’s easy to mess up the timings (sprite 0’s flag is not cleared after polling it, which leads to ‘duplicated’ positives <sup id="bibref:31"><a href="#bib:graphics-chibiakumas" role="doc-biblioref">[31]</a></sup>). Furthermore, as this routine repeats indefinitely, it can be quite costly (in terms of CPU cycles) to execute. On the bright side, later mappers took over this function by employing automatic interrupts that are triggered whenever an arbitrary scan-line is hit <sup id="bibref:32"><a href="#bib:graphics-nesdoug" role="doc-biblioref">[32]</a></sup> (a much more efficient technique), which significantly improved the visual capabilities of Super Mario Bros 3, for instance.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-1-3-sprite-layer">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-1-5-result">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-1-5-result"><h4 id="tab-1-5-result" class="tab-title">Result</h4><figure class="float-side pixel"><a class="pixel" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/ppu_mario/result.b4d077e7fb855c96b087f8cb5fdda12a4eb258758320dd3cb747a4f8b0a55623.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="256" height="240" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/ppu_mario/result.b4d077e7fb855c96b087f8cb5fdda12a4eb258758320dd3cb747a4f8b0a55623.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Tada!</figcaption></figure><p>Once the frame is finished, it’s time to move on to the next one!</p><p>However, the CPU can’t modify any table currently in use by the PPU, otherwise, artefacts may show up on the screen. So, when all scan-lines are completed, the PPU triggers the <strong>Vertical Blank</strong> (V-Blank) interrupt on the CPU <sup id="bibref:33"><a href="#bib:graphics-vblank" role="doc-biblioref">[33]</a></sup>. This notifies the game that it can start updating the tables without tearing the picture currently displayed. At that moment, the CRT’s beam is pointing below the visible area of the screen, into the overscan (or bottom border area).</p><p>Only a handful of PPU registers can be updated outside the V-Blank window <sup id="bibref:34"><a href="#bib:graphics-outside_vblank" role="doc-biblioref">[34]</a></sup>, which explains the ability to scroll the background layer mid-frame.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-1-4-background-split">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next pre">Next »</a></div></div></div></div><h3 id="secrets-and-limitations">Secrets and limitations</h3><p>If you’re thinking that a frame-buffer system with memory allocated to store the full frame would have been preferable: RAM costs were prohibitively high, and the console’s goal was to be affordable. Let me now show you why this design still proved to be both efficient and flexible.</p><div class="tabs"><ul class="tab-links"><li id="tab-2-1-multi-scrolling-link" class="active"><a href="#tab-2-1-multi-scrolling">Multi-Scrolling</a></li><li id="tab-2-2-tile-swapping-link"><a href="#tab-2-2-tile-swapping">Tile-Swapping</a></li><li id="tab-2-3-curious-behaviour-link"><a href="#tab-2-3-curious-behaviour">Curious behaviour</a></li></ul><div class="tab-content"><div class="tab active body-side" id="tab-2-1-multi-scrolling"><h4 id="tab-2-1-multi-scrolling" class="tab-title">Multi-Scrolling</h4><figure class="float-side pixel"><a class="pixel" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/secrets/multiscrolling_mirror.69ee2c1e8f9336fb7c94b85f8e5ce5ed83f0f57f25bdb12c121bd1f7e755e99f.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="512" height="480" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/secrets/multiscrolling_mirror.69ee2c1e8f9336fb7c94b85f8e5ce5ed83f0f57f25bdb12c121bd1f7e755e99f.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">In this level of Super Mario Bros. 2, the Nametable is set up for vertical scrolling (horizontal mirroring).</figcaption></figure><figure class="float-side pixel"><a class="pixel" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/secrets/multiscrolling.0b5ffd79e4463beb3bffbbf8781de6be84fbfbaedbf2de370177527307cef6f1.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="256" height="240" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/secrets/multiscrolling.0b5ffd79e4463beb3bffbbf8781de6be84fbfbaedbf2de370177527307cef6f1.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">With Super Mario Bros. 3, Mario can run and fly. Thus, the PPU needs to scroll diagonally. Notice the right edge is showing the wrong colour palette, and the left edge has a mask applied.</figcaption></figure><p>Some games require the main character to move vertically; therefore, the nametable is set up with <strong>horizontal mirroring</strong>. Other games need their character to move left and right, and so implement <strong>vertical mirroring</strong> instead.</p><p>Either type of mirroring allows the PPU to update background tiles without the user noticing, as there is ample of space to scroll while new tiles are being rendered at a distance.</p><p>But what happens if the character needs to move diagonally? The PPU can scroll in any direction; however, without extra VRAM, the edges are forced to share the same colour palette (remember that tiles are grouped in blocks).</p><p>This explains why some games like <em>Super Mario Bros. 3</em> show strange graphics at the right edge of the screen while Mario moves (the game is set up for vertical scrolling) <sup id="bibref:35"><a href="#bib:graphics-seam" role="doc-biblioref">[35]</a></sup>. It’s possible that they needed to minimise the hardware cost per cartridge, as this game already bundles a powerful mapper.</p><p>As an interesting <em>fix</em>: the PPU allowed developers to apply a vertical mask on top of tiles, effectively concealing part of the glitchy area.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev pre">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-2-2-tile-swapping">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-2-2-tile-swapping"><h4 id="tab-2-2-tile-swapping" class="tab-title">Tile-Swapping</h4><figure class="tabs nested float-side pixel"><ul class="tab-links nested"><li id="nestedtab-6-1-early-link" class="active"><a href="#nestedtab-6-1-early">Early</a></li><li id="nestedtab-6-2-late-link"><a href="#nestedtab-6-2-late">Late</a></li><li id="nestedtab-6-3-displayed-link"><a href="#nestedtab-6-3-displayed">Displayed</a></li></ul><figure class="tab active nested" id="nestedtab-6-1-early"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/secrets/multiplexing_1.d8e6b0730b39458e7d6306c71b3a75c559b4e4bdc8ea7542be7c323d05f856e6.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="256" height="240" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/secrets/multiplexing_1.d8e6b0730b39458e7d6306c71b3a75c559b4e4bdc8ea7542be7c323d05f856e6.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Early scan lines.</figcaption></figure><figure class="tab nested" id="nestedtab-6-2-late"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/secrets/multiplexing_2.caf48911e860280c482d8264f49007d9d3b1efafbee0f26024be7ff1a1f65395.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="256" height="240" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/secrets/multiplexing_2.caf48911e860280c482d8264f49007d9d3b1efafbee0f26024be7ff1a1f65395.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Late scan lines.</figcaption></figure><figure class="tab nested" id="nestedtab-6-3-displayed"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/secrets/multiplexing_complete.316fb464f79dfeab19f2f9769cc152185d5c9401f8210dd8ffb2ac4ed429d820.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="256" height="240" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/secrets/multiplexing_complete.316fb464f79dfeab19f2f9769cc152185d5c9401f8210dd8ffb2ac4ed429d820.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Actual frame displayed to the user.</figcaption></figure><figcaption class="caption group">Hypothetical frames rendered using tiles available during specific scan lines.</figcaption></figure><p>Another remarkable feature of Super Mario Bros. 3 is the number of graphics it can display.</p><p>This game displays more background tiles than strictly permitted. How does it achieve this? By taking two screen captures at different times while the display is generated, we can see that the final frame is actually composed of <em>two</em> distinct frames.</p><p>This is another wizardry of the MMC3 mapper, which not only addresses extra space in the Program ROM, but also extends the Character ROM space by connecting <strong>two separate Character chips</strong>. By determining which part of the screen the PPU is requesting, the mapper redirects to one chip or the other, thereby allowing more unique tiles on-screen than was originally supported <sup id="bibref:36"><a href="#bib:graphics-n3s" role="doc-biblioref">[36]</a></sup>.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-2-1-multi-scrolling">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-2-3-curious-behaviour">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-2-3-curious-behaviour"><h4 id="tab-2-3-curious-behaviour" class="tab-title">Curious behaviour</h4><p>Throughout my research, I came across many interesting articles that explain unusual behaviour of the PPU, so I thought to mention a few here:</p><ul><li>Unlike the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/master-system/#graphics">Master System’s VDP</a>, which generates RGB colours that are subsequently encoded into NTSC/PAL signals for broadcasting, the <strong>NES’ PPU does all at once</strong> <sup id="bibref:37"><a href="#bib:graphics-palettes" role="doc-biblioref">[37]</a></sup>. Hence, there isn’t a one-to-one correspondence between the colours of the PPU master palette and the standard RGB colourspace (widely adopted by present technology). This leaves some room for interpretation and, as a consequence, various emulators may display a different palette.<ul><li>The discrepancies between RGB palettes can be observed using Tim Worthington’s DIY kit, which adds RGB signal output to the NES. This also houses a switch to choose between three predefined palettes <sup id="bibref:38"><a href="#bib:graphics-nesrgb" role="doc-biblioref">[38]</a></sup>.</li></ul></li><li>The master palette contains a <strong>‘cursed’ colour</strong> (<code>$0D</code>), which might disrupt the NTSC TV signal <sup id="bibref:39"><a href="#bib:graphics-cursed_colour" role="doc-biblioref">[39]</a></sup>. Well, what happens is that some TVs mistake the signal for displaying that colour as the blanking signal, which may cause flickering.</li><li>The PPU relies on DRAM to store its Object Attribute Memory (OAM). Now, unlike SRAM, DRAM must be refreshed constantly to prevent data loss. Conversely, <strong>the PPU doesn’t refresh DRAM when it’s not rendering the frame</strong> <sup id="bibref:40"><a href="#bib:graphics-oam" role="doc-biblioref">[40]</a></sup>. This typically occurs during vertical blanking. For this reason, it is advised to always update OAM during vertical blanking, since the non-refreshing period (happening during V-blank) will have corrupted part of the table.<ul><li>The PPU variant for PAL systems is unaffected by this, as it does refresh during V-Blank (which lasts longer on PAL systems).</li></ul></li></ul><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-2-2-tile-swapping">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next pre">Next »</a></div></div></div></div><hr><h2 id="audio">Audio</h2><p>A dedicated component called <strong>Audio Processing Unit</strong> (APU) provides this service <sup id="bibref:41"><a href="#bib:audio-apu" role="doc-biblioref">[41]</a></sup>. Ricoh embedded it inside the CPU chip, presumably to prevent unlicensed cloning of both the CPU and APU.</p><h3 id="functionality">Functionality</h3><p>This audio circuitry is commonly referred to as a <strong>Programmable Sound Generator</strong> (PSG), which vaguely implies that it can only produce a predefined set of waveforms. This is <em>mostly</em> true in this case.</p><p>The APU sequences audio data across <strong>five channels</strong>, each reserved for a specific waveform or signal. The channels contain different properties that alter the waveform’s pitch, sound, volume and duration. They are continuously mixed and transmitted through the output audio signal.</p><p>The APU’s functionality is exposed through memory addresses. The CPU reads the music-related data found in the Program ROM and programs the APU accordingly.</p><p>Furthermore, the Famicom model implements extra cartridge pins that send the mixed audio signal to the cartridge, so the latter can mix it with <strong>extra channels</strong> (requiring additional chips) <sup id="bibref:42"><a href="#bib:general-cartridge" role="doc-biblioref">[42]</a></sup>.</p><p>Let’s now review the five channels the APU provides <sup id="bibref:43"><a href="#bib:audio-review" role="doc-biblioref">[43]</a></sup>:</p><div class="tabs"><ul class="tab-links"><li id="tab-3-1-pulse-link" class="active"><a href="#tab-3-1-pulse">Pulse</a></li><li id="tab-3-2-triangle-link"><a href="#tab-3-2-triangle">Triangle</a></li><li id="tab-3-3-noise-link"><a href="#tab-3-3-noise">Noise</a></li><li id="tab-3-4-sample-link"><a href="#tab-3-4-sample">Sample</a></li></ul><div class="tab-content"><div class="tab active body-side" id="tab-3-1-pulse"><h4 id="tab-3-1-pulse" class="tab-title">Pulse</h4><figure class="tabs nested float-side"><ul class="tab-links nested"><li id="nestedtab-7-1-pulse-1-link"><a href="#nestedtab-7-1-pulse-1">Pulse 1</a></li><li id="nestedtab-7-2-pulse-2-link" class="active"><a href="#nestedtab-7-2-pulse-2">Pulse 2</a></li><li id="nestedtab-7-3-complete-link"><a href="#nestedtab-7-3-complete">Complete</a></li></ul><figure class="tab nested" id="nestedtab-7-1-pulse-1"><video poster="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/video_posters/pulse_single_1.a3bf966e4d9d6d8cc2518c0f432fabc3dc8e6166485948f3876260fb796837df.jpg" preload="none" width="1024" height="768" style="width:100%;height:auto" src="https://www.copetti.org/videos/consoles/nes/pulse_single_1.f205d34f964fc16cb110c1e40de0b366b8ef247e5a2ac6c04e5d0ba26cdca0ed.mp4" controls="" controllist="nodownload">
No support for video.</video><figcaption class="caption">Pulse 1 channel.</figcaption></figure><figure class="tab active nested" id="nestedtab-7-2-pulse-2"><video poster="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/video_posters/pulse_single_2.ccc384e4780ad46c7c4d1686be6f02a93e0b6a750e527da4262106e77e9f6eed.jpg" preload="none" width="1024" height="768" style="width:100%;height:auto" src="https://www.copetti.org/videos/consoles/nes/pulse_single_2.16bc5d021b41e881a1c55fc8f60343e5c6564faeeb642cc0269998a8df9578df.mp4" controls="" controllist="nodownload">
No support for video.</video><figcaption class="caption">Pulse 2 channel.</figcaption></figure><figure class="tab nested" id="nestedtab-7-3-complete"><video poster="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/video_posters/pulse_full.33b15fe5eae4d5429358f096252fc30373d69e53ec304627c7c3205df9474583.jpg" preload="none" width="1024" height="768" style="width:100%;height:auto" src="https://www.copetti.org/videos/consoles/nes/pulse_full.293364b3f00983afba016686d2bb6f9c58f76668e447d2fe4935a4fce1c8d116.mp4" controls="" controllist="nodownload">
No support for video.</video><figcaption class="caption">All audio channels.</figcaption></figure><figcaption class="caption group">Oscilloscope display of a music score from Mother (1989).</figcaption></figure><p>The first <strong>two channels</strong> produce <strong>pulse waves</strong> <sup id="bibref:44"><a href="#bib:audio-apupulse" role="doc-biblioref">[44]</a></sup>. When heard, they exhibit a very distinct <em>beep</em> sound that is mainly used for <strong>melody or sound effects</strong>. By varying the pulse width (also known as the <strong>duty cycle</strong>), the respective sequencer can generate three types of pulse waves. The circuits are also connected to a <strong>sweep unit</strong> (allowing to bend the pitch) and an <strong>envelope generator</strong> to lower the volume over time (commonly referred to as <strong>decay</strong>).</p><p>Most games use one pulse channel for melody and the other for accompaniment. You’ll often find that when a game needs to play a sound effect, the accompaniment channel is temporarily switched to play the effect before returning to its original role. This prevents interrupting the melody during gameplay.</p><p>I believe it’s fair to say that pulse waves are one of the emblems of this generation of consoles. I assume their adoption was primarily driven by cost-effectiveness: the (limited) CPU can only process a finite amount of data at a time, and pulse waves are ideal because they require few parameters to play simple melodies (which, in turn, frees up CPU cycles for other operations).</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev pre">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-3-2-triangle">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-3-2-triangle"><h4 id="tab-3-2-triangle" class="tab-title">Triangle</h4><figure class="tabs nested float-side"><ul class="tab-links nested"><li id="nestedtab-8-1-triangle-link" class="active"><a href="#nestedtab-8-1-triangle">Triangle</a></li><li id="nestedtab-8-2-complete-link"><a href="#nestedtab-8-2-complete">Complete</a></li></ul><figure class="tab active nested" id="nestedtab-8-1-triangle"><video poster="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/video_posters/triangle_single.eb70dfba319adfad533b0d20ea9c0da196efee7abe9ec565195435cd5b84acbe.jpg" preload="none" width="1024" height="768" style="width:100%;height:auto" src="https://www.copetti.org/videos/consoles/nes/triangle_single.0971f7daf46f0be9115612a40848cf550e9f2416a7e025d0f80baadce2a0805f.mp4" controls="" controllist="nodownload">
No support for video.</video><figcaption class="caption">Triangle channel.</figcaption></figure><figure class="tab nested" id="nestedtab-8-2-complete"><video poster="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/video_posters/triangle_full.b838d9a30ac644605d192e789806bdb9b542208a4310c2adc3cc7a350516f894.jpg" preload="none" width="1024" height="768" style="width:100%;height:auto" src="https://www.copetti.org/videos/consoles/nes/triangle_full.c46ea73f38caf0b4dfe45675834acfd621207eab79e79be9fa9aa4630d3bd4d9.mp4" controls="" controllist="nodownload">
No support for video.</video><figcaption class="caption">All audio channels.</figcaption></figure><figcaption class="caption group">Oscilloscope display of a music score from Mother (1989).</figcaption></figure><p>One of the specialities of the APU, when compared to the competition, is its ability to produce <strong>triangle waves</strong>. These are often used as a <strong>bassline</strong> for melodies. Additionally, by dramatically modifying its pitch, it can also be used for <strong>percussion</strong>.</p><p>The APU has one channel reserved for this type of wave. Behind the scenes, a dedicated sequencer takes 32 cycles to generate a triangle signal <sup id="bibref:45"><a href="#bib:audio-aputriangle" role="doc-biblioref">[45]</a></sup>; this limitation causes the resulting triangle waveform to resemble a step ladder.</p><p>On the other side, the respective circuitry does not provide volume control. In any case, some games discovered alternative methods by fiddling with the mixer’s volume control.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-3-1-pulse">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-3-3-noise">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-3-3-noise"><h4 id="tab-3-3-noise" class="tab-title">Noise</h4><figure class="tabs nested float-side"><ul class="tab-links nested"><li id="nestedtab-9-1-noise-link" class="active"><a href="#nestedtab-9-1-noise">Noise</a></li><li id="nestedtab-9-2-complete-link"><a href="#nestedtab-9-2-complete">Complete</a></li></ul><figure class="tab active nested" id="nestedtab-9-1-noise"><video poster="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/video_posters/noise_single.4c3f2f6e882c9ad5e6c1a09284124a0025bf3bacce8adf435559d2b4a4f2c878.jpg" preload="none" width="1024" height="768" style="width:100%;height:auto" src="https://www.copetti.org/videos/consoles/nes/noise_single.6fa2d7af572ccf16582591bc9c85fffc5a2856b72ee92ce66731dfe1921d8635.mp4" controls="" controllist="nodownload">
No support for video.</video><figcaption class="caption">Noise channel.</figcaption></figure><figure class="tab nested" id="nestedtab-9-2-complete"><video poster="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/video_posters/noise_full.2a21daee093171fb4c13b5801c84f385c6b1fad6d4c56f8201a5d4082ec862bc.jpg" preload="none" width="1024" height="768" style="width:100%;height:auto" src="https://www.copetti.org/videos/consoles/nes/noise_full.0e80e5712b4a42f4c30e8c1bf99b5ebeb59157e10d6f514070c59449a31099d9.mp4" controls="" controllist="nodownload">
No support for video.</video><figcaption class="caption">All audio channels.</figcaption></figure><figcaption class="caption group">Oscilloscope display of a music score from Mother (1989).</figcaption></figure><p>The concept of ‘Noise’ refers to a series of waveforms that lack any discernible pattern or order. In turn, our ears interpret it as white static. That said, the APU allocates one channel to play different kinds of noise.</p><p>Behind the scenes, the noise generator relies on an envelope generator (similar to the Pulse channel) that is randomly muted by an OR gate <sup id="bibref:46"><a href="#bib:audio-apunoise" role="doc-biblioref">[46]</a></sup>. The condition for muting is determined by the value of a 15-bit shift register connected to a feedback loop. All in all, this makes the circuitry output a signal with <em>pseudo-unpredictable</em> patterns, resulting in noise.</p><p>For control, four bits adjust the period of the envelope generator, while one bit modifies the ‘Mode’ of the shift register. This layout provides 32 noise presets. Half (16) of these presets generate <strong>clean static</strong>, and the other half produce <strong>robotic static</strong>.</p><p>Generally speaking, games utilise the noise channel for percussion or ambient effects.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-3-2-triangle">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-3-4-sample">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-3-4-sample"><h4 id="tab-3-4-sample" class="tab-title">Sample</h4><figure class="tabs nested float-side"><ul class="tab-links nested"><li id="nestedtab-10-1-sample-link" class="active"><a href="#nestedtab-10-1-sample">Sample</a></li><li id="nestedtab-10-2-complete-link"><a href="#nestedtab-10-2-complete">Complete</a></li></ul><figure class="tab active nested" id="nestedtab-10-1-sample"><video poster="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/video_posters/sample_single.9cbff9769098850062b38c7f7b8e152ffd7216d402ba04f45d37067b6308235a.jpg" preload="none" width="1024" height="768" style="width:100%;height:auto" src="https://www.copetti.org/videos/consoles/nes/sample_single.8ba08475938e718f72e70c27983df6f5d98cb2d2117488919eda0213d015d8de.mp4" controls="" controllist="nodownload">
No support for video.</video><figcaption class="caption">Sample channel.</figcaption></figure><figure class="tab nested" id="nestedtab-10-2-complete"><video poster="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/video_posters/sample_full.a2bfaa924fcf7ceaaaf04e4be0c08e806a482349bea92fd2e352415b0f3e714f.jpg" preload="none" width="1024" height="768" style="width:100%;height:auto" src="https://www.copetti.org/videos/consoles/nes/sample_full.f02be08f448413ccd5ba2299a16b4efbf243c6f1c3767f40aff06a18757630ae.mp4" controls="" controllist="nodownload">
No support for video.</video><figcaption class="caption">All audio channels.</figcaption></figure><figcaption class="caption group">Oscilloscope display of a music score from Mother (1989).</figcaption></figure><p>Samples are recorded pieces of music that can be replayed. As you can see, samples are not confined to a single waveform, but they consume a lot more storage space.</p><p>The APU has one channel dedicated to samples. Here, samples are limited to <strong>7-bit resolution</strong> (encoded with values from <code>0</code> to <code>127</code>) and a <strong>~15.74 kHz sampling rate</strong> <sup id="bibref:47"><a href="#bib:audio-2a03ref" role="doc-biblioref">[47]</a></sup>. To program this channel, games can either stream 7-bit values (which steals significant cycles and storage) or use <strong>delta modulation</strong> to encode only the variation between consecutive samples.</p><p>The delta modulation system in the APU only accepts 1-bit values, meaning games can only indicated whether the sample increments or decrements by <code>1</code> each time the counter kicks in. Thus, at the cost of fidelity, delta modulation can save games from having to stream continuous values to the APU.</p><p>Since programming this channel takes longer space and CPU cycles, games typically store small pieces (like drum sounds) that can be replayed repeatedly. Be as it may, throughout the NES’ lifespan, numerous developers have come up with clever uses for this channel.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-3-3-noise">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next pre">Next »</a></div></div></div></div><h3 id="secrets-and-limitations-1">Secrets and limitations</h3><p>While the APU could not match the audio quality of vinyl, cassette or CD, programmers did find ways to extend its capabilities, largely thanks to the modular architecture of the NES.</p><div class="tabs"><ul class="tab-links"><li id="tab-4-1-extra-channels-link" class="active"><a href="#tab-4-1-extra-channels">Extra Channels</a></li><li id="tab-4-2-tremolo-link"><a href="#tab-4-2-tremolo">Tremolo</a></li></ul><div class="tab-content"><div class="tab active body-side" id="tab-4-1-extra-channels"><h4 id="tab-4-1-extra-channels" class="tab-title">Extra Channels</h4><figure class="tabs nested float-side"><ul class="tab-links nested"><li id="nestedtab-11-1-american-link" class="active"><a href="#nestedtab-11-1-american">American</a></li><li id="nestedtab-11-2-japanese-link"><a href="#nestedtab-11-2-japanese">Japanese</a></li></ul><figure class="tab active nested" id="nestedtab-11-1-american"><video poster="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/video_posters/castlevania_usa.a721a2d6ff1b9d2864706183fdd8e1ee0d869459f4a5f9f735dfb76cdc81906d.jpg" preload="none" width="1024" height="768" style="width:100%;height:auto" src="https://www.copetti.org/videos/consoles/nes/castlevania_usa.d5510ae5914b06dddce705fe1c7dd4fdaa199f097777c0e708c39bf0190b6ac7.mp4" controls="" controllist="nodownload">
No support for video.</video><figcaption class="caption">Castlevania III (USA/Europe, 1989).</figcaption></figure><figure class="tab nested" id="nestedtab-11-2-japanese"><video poster="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/video_posters/castlevania_jap.b5be574009e466e7de35775f5af1364c6409653955b2df6c8d78bb69b7914610.jpg" preload="none" width="1024" height="1024" style="width:100%;height:auto" src="https://www.copetti.org/videos/consoles/nes/castlevania_jap.f8f9425c6fc4325b40e6b60fd5760f70236b5bac0fa2b607f7533c34119d1d95.mp4" controls="" controllist="nodownload">
No support for video.</video><figcaption class="caption">Akumajō Densetsu (Japan, 1989).</figcaption></figure><figcaption class="caption group">Oscilloscope display of the same music score across the two regions.</figcaption></figure><p>Remember that the Famicom provided exclusive cartridge pins available for sound expansion? Well, games like <em>Castlevania 3</em> took advantage of this feature by incorporating an additional chip called <strong>Konami VRC6</strong>, which introduced <strong>two extra pulse waves and a sawtooth wave</strong> to the mix.</p><p>The two examples illustrate the difference between the Japanese and the American versions of the game. The Japanese variant, running on the Famicom, benefits from the enhanced audio capabilities, while the American version, designed for the NES, is constrained by the five predefined channels.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev pre">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-4-2-tremolo">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-4-2-tremolo"><h4 id="tab-4-2-tremolo" class="tab-title">Tremolo</h4><figure class="float-side"><video poster="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/video_posters/tremolo_full.11e7069daaa992af7f9c14fab9b84af915e44e6a608119102ce05dcdf035b0ce.jpg" preload="none" width="1024" height="768" style="width:100%;height:auto" src="https://www.copetti.org/videos/consoles/nes/tremolo_full.854aa66d852edff15f3970ad188b712de2c001f9c537fdfc08be4329d69e37be.mp4" controls="" controllist="nodownload">
No support for video.</video><figcaption class="caption">Oscilloscope view of Final Fantasy III (1990).</figcaption></figure><p>Rather than increasing cartridge costs, some games prioritised creativity over technology to simulate additional channels.</p><p>For instance, Final Fantasy III came up with the idea of using tremolo effects to create the illusion of extra channels.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-4-1-extra-channels">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next pre">Next »</a></div></div></div></div><h3 id="a-more-refined-observation">A more refined observation</h3><p>Now that you’ve had a glimpse of what the APU is capable of, let me show you a more precise method for observing how its sound behaves. This will not only complement what you already know about the APU but also provide a more objective examination.</p><p>First things first, let’s start with a brief introduction to sound theory.</p><p>Thanks to the principles of <strong>Fourier Analysis</strong>, we can decompose every single sound we hear into a <strong>sum of sine waves</strong> with different frequencies and amplitudes <sup id="bibref:48"><a href="#bib:audio-complexwaveforms" role="doc-biblioref">[48]</a></sup>. The lowest-frequency sine wave is called the <strong>fundamental</strong>, while the others are referred to as <strong>overtones</strong>. If you add the fundamental wave and its overtones, you get the original sound back. Having said that, with sounds that have a recognisable pitch, you’ll find most (if not all) overtones have frequencies that are multiples of the fundamental frequency. Thus, these overtones are called <strong>harmonics</strong> <sup id="bibref:49"><a href="#bib:audio-harmonics" role="doc-biblioref">[49]</a></sup>.</p><p>Harmonics will be a recurring topic in this section, as waveforms such as pulses, triangles, and sawtooths adhere to a formula that determines the harmonics they must contain. Otherwise, these waveforms might deviate from their ‘perfect’ shape.</p><h4 id="introduction-to-spectrograms">Introduction to spectrograms</h4><p>As sine waves are now the key ingredient that can make up any sound, we can now analyse the sounds that we hear by their sine waves. Now, for any kind of data analysis, there’s nothing more convenient than plotting a graph to organise vast amounts of information. Well, in the case of sound analysis, we’ve got <strong>Spectrograms</strong>. These encode all the information from an audio sample in a single plot. The X-axis denotes time (in seconds), the Y-axis denotes the frequencies (in Hz) of sine waves produced during that time, and the Z-axis (intensity of each dot) denotes the power/loudness (in decibels) of each frequency.</p><figure class="centered-container"><video poster="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/video_posters/spectrogram_example.eb6cc666991cfb9cfe5a7a6c3e55abfb5b7c955be348b41ff0156f52dbd7af5d.jpg" preload="none" width="1280" height="720" style="width:100%;height:auto" src="https://www.copetti.org/videos/consoles/nes/spectrogram_example.3ef3d7aa550b39fffa8313be83dc3aac323601775e24fe4ddf6b71ca4b41b32f.mp4" controls="" controllist="nodownload">
No support for video.</video><figcaption class="caption">Example of spectrogram visualising six seconds of a Pulse channel.</figcaption></figure><p>As you can observe from this example, each horizontal line (a.k.a. sequences of dots) corresponds to a sine wave (the lowest is the fundamental, while the rest are the harmonics) and their intensity indicates the amplitude. With this in mind, we can extract the following information:</p><ul><li>Over time, horizontal lines tend to drastically displace. That’s the pitch of the Pulse channel changing.</li><li>The start of each note is loud (the dots are vibrant) followed by a quick quell. That’s the APU’s envelope control in action.<ul><li>Moreover, at the end of the decay period, a vertical line shows up. It’s quite brief so it’s not easily audible but, in any case, that’s noise (a short popping sound) and I suspect it’s a deficiency of the APU.</li></ul></li><li>Holding a note for more than 0.25 seconds makes <strong>vibrato</strong> emerge (continuous fluctuations in the Y-axis). I’m not sure if that’s intentional (using the sweep function) or an adverse effect of the APU.</li></ul><p>Notice how most of these observations are not easily derived by just listening to an audio sample; this is the reason for writing this section.</p><h4 id="plotting-the-apu">Plotting the APU</h4><p>To study the NES’ APU, I’ve compiled five spectrograms, each corresponding to one of the APU’s channels, using the previous examples. Alongside them, you’ll find my attempt at unravelling what the data is exhibiting.</p><p>Before we start, I must confess that, to gather the data without inaccuracies (such as extra noise), some compromises were made. The recordings were obtained using a Windows program called ‘towave’, which uses <strong>band-limited synthesis</strong> to solve a fundamental problem with the emulation of PSG-based audio chips. Essentially, pulses, triangles and sawtooths consist of <strong>infinite harmonics</strong>. However, this doesn’t mix well with modern sound cards which are limited to 44.1 kHz samples. Thus, a technique called ‘band-limited synthesis’ is employed to select the right harmonics within the sound card’s limitations. All in all, this technique provides a feasible balance between performance, accuracy, and aliasing prevention. However, the data may not be 100% identical to its analogue counterpart (which, by contrast, would also introduce other issues, like noise from the recording equipment), but I believe it is to an acceptable degree and, most importantly, does the job for this section of the article.</p><p>That being said, let’s get on with the analysis.</p><div class="tabs"><ul class="tab-links"><li id="tab-5-1-pulse-link" class="active"><a href="#tab-5-1-pulse">Pulse</a></li><li id="tab-5-2-triangle-link"><a href="#tab-5-2-triangle">Triangle</a></li><li id="tab-5-3-noise-link"><a href="#tab-5-3-noise">Noise</a></li><li id="tab-5-4-sample-link"><a href="#tab-5-4-sample">Sample</a></li><li id="tab-5-5-sawtooth-link"><a href="#tab-5-5-sawtooth">Sawtooth</a></li></ul><div class="tab-content"><div class="tab active body-side" id="tab-5-1-pulse"><h5 id="tab-5-1-pulse" class="tab-title">Pulse</h5><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/spectrograms/eb0_pulse_nes.3a55c1442998128eb5f5f9bc6dbc4660577f91eb10816acdbe57dcb8d01b45f2.png"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/spectrograms/eb0_pulse_nes.3a55c1442998128eb5f5f9bc6dbc4660577f91eb10816acdbe57dcb8d01b45f2_hu_65675e5edc1bec08.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/spectrograms/eb0_pulse_nes.3a55c1442998128eb5f5f9bc6dbc4660577f91eb10816acdbe57dcb8d01b45f2_hu_709adb9534440109.webp 800w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/spectrograms/eb0_pulse_nes.3a55c1442998128eb5f5f9bc6dbc4660577f91eb10816acdbe57dcb8d01b45f2_hu_291b18d4cf0d2d2d.webp 1294w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="1294" height="990" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/spectrograms/eb0_pulse_nes.3a55c1442998128eb5f5f9bc6dbc4660577f91eb10816acdbe57dcb8d01b45f2.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Spectrogram of the Pulse 1 channel.</figcaption></figure><p>The theory says that a pulse tone only contains odd harmonics. In other words, the fundamental is combined with its third harmonic, fifth and so forth. Moreover, each harmonic decreases its amplitude the further it is from the fundamental. The amplitude formula is <code>amplitude = 1 ÷ harmonic number</code> <sup id="bibref:50"><a href="#bib:audio-pulse" role="doc-biblioref">[50]</a></sup>.</p><p>Hence, notice how the intensity of each harmonic on the spectrogram dims the higher it is on the Y-axis. However, the APU’s pulse waves also seem to exhibit the aforementioned vibrato effect which intensifies at each harmonic number. Moreover, areas of the spectrogram that should be empty of any sound contain hushed overtones (possibly the result of noise and other imperfections).</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev pre">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-5-2-triangle">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-5-2-triangle"><h5 id="tab-5-2-triangle" class="tab-title">Triangle</h5><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/spectrograms/eb0_triangle_nes.aba5614553cf6f43d5409f512e922a9d988457ba37447c8765cd18a858d765b6.png"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/spectrograms/eb0_triangle_nes.aba5614553cf6f43d5409f512e922a9d988457ba37447c8765cd18a858d765b6_hu_7addfb40e8743b3c.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/nes/spectrograms/eb0_triangle_nes.aba5614553cf6f43d5409f512e922a9d988457ba37447c8765cd18a858d765b6_hu_db814c331f6f017f.webp 800w,
